sermons.speaker: Craig Coborne

sermons.text: Okay, the passage this morning is in Isaiah chapter forty-two, verses one to nine. Behold, my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen one in whom I del in whom my soul delights. I have put my spirit upon him. He will bring forth justice to the nations. He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor make his voice heard in the street. A bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not extinguish. He will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not be disheartened or crushed until he has established justice in the earth, and the coastlands will wait expectantly for his law. Thus says God the Lord, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and its offspring, who gives breath to the people on it. And spirit to those who walk in it. I am the Lord. I have called you in righteousness. I will also hold you by the hand and watch over you, and I will appoint you as a covenant to the people. and as a light to the nations, to open blind eyes, to bring bring out prisoners from the dungeon, and those who dwell in darkness from the prison. I am the Lord. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images. Behold, the former things have come to pass. Now I declare new things. Before they spring forth, I proclaim them to you. Thus far God's word. One of the things that we learned early on in our time in Japan is that Japanese people have a dislike for making strong statements. And in fact, in the Japanese language, there's a special verb form for making weak assertions. So for example, if you wanted to say it's raining now, you'd say, Amedes. But to say that it will rain tomorrow, even a professional meteorologist, even an expert in the field, would use the weak assertion form. Ameidesho. When Japanese people state their opinions, they use this weak assertion form in order to take into consideration that someone else may have a different opinion. It's expensive. Takaidosho. It's difficult, muscashi to show. Even parents, when they correct their children, use the weak assertion form when explaining why the wrong behavior was unacceptable. It's dangerous. Abunaidesho. It's rude. And so since there is in Japanese culture this dislike for making strong statements, You probably won't be surprised to learn that some of the strong statements in the Bible are stumbling blocks for Japanese people. As we read the Bible with Japanese people, often they have a very favorable response to what they see. They love the golden rule. Do to others as you would have them do to you. They like the second greatest commandment. Love your neighbor as yourself. However, the first sign of trouble usually comes when we get to John 14. 6. Where Jesus says, I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. This very strong statement is difficult for Japanese people to accept. It flies in the face of a famous Japanese proverb that says that there are many paths to the top of Mount Fuji, by which they mean one way is just as good as another. The Japanese are a people who had no difficulty accepting the Chinese religion of Buddhism or the religion of Buddhism that the Chinese brought to Japan in the 6th century. They simply mixed aspects of Buddhism. with aspects of Shinto, the native religion of Japan. And so the result is that when you hear figures about religion in Japan, you hear things like this. Seventy-five percent of Japanese are Buddhist, and 85% of Japanese are Shinto. Yeah, I was a math professor, and so those are a math teacher, so those uh those numbers sort of blow my mind a little. Incidentally, less than one half of one percent of Japanese are evangelical Christians. And so many Japanese would be happy to take the things that they like from the Bible and throw that into the mix as well. But the God of the Bible could never tolerate worship for him being mixed with the idolatries of Buddhism and of Shinto. Such eclecticism is repulsive to him. He says in the Bible, This is what the Lord says, Israel's king and redeemer, the Lord Almighty. I am the first, and I am the last. I am the Lord, and there is no other. Apart from me, there is no God. Or, from this morning's text, I am the Lord. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, or my praise to graven images. Recently, we experienced this clash between the strong statements of the Bible and the Japanese dislike for strong statements with a woman named Mrs. Inoue. Mrs. Ineley had studied in the United States during her college years. Now she was back in Japan, she was married, and had a kindergarten-aged son. As she was living in Japan, she began to feel her fluency in English starting to slip away, and she didn't want that to continue. And so she decided that now that her son was in kindergarten, she had time to do something about that. So when she heard about my wife Ree's uh Wednesday morning English Bible study, she asked if she could come. At that Bible study she met a group of women, only one of whom was a Christian, although another one has since become a Christian. Some of the women she met there were genuinely seeking spiritually. Others were just intellectually curious about what the Bible said, and others just wanted to speak English. But it was clear in Mrs. Inoue's case from early on that she was really thinking about what she was reading in the Bible. She asked very sincere questions. She freely shared her response to things that she was reading. Some of the things she found very appealing, others she just didn't seem to understand at all But soon we began hearing her asserting biblical truths as her own convictions. She believed that Jesus was God. She believed that he had been raised from the dead. There were times when instead of Ree or me explaining the truth to the group from the Bible, it was Mrs. Inoue explaining the truth to the group. And just before we left Japan to come back to the U. S. , she volunteered to host the English Bible study, which had been meeting in our home, in her home, while we were gone. But there was this one issue that kept coming up a few times. It was her grandfather. Not that Mrs. Inoue was concerned that her grandfather would disapprove of her growing interest in biblical things, although that is very common in Japan. In Mrs. Inway's case, she never knew her grandfather. He died before she was born. But she believes that her grandfather watches over her. She says that he helps her. She gives an example of a time when she had an important meeting the next morning and she forgot to set her alarm clock. In the middle of the night, she suddenly woke up and she realized that she'd not set her alarm clock, and so she was able to set it and to be at her appointment on time. She's convinced that it was her grandfather who caused her to wake up in the middle of the night. She prays to him during difficult times. She thinks of him as a kind of a God. And it's at this point that some of those strong statements from the Bible are difficult from Mrs. Inoue. I am the Lord, and there is no other. Apart from me, there is no God. I will not give my glory to another, or my praise to graven images. Mrs. Enoy is a very kind lady, and she's been very good to us. We love her, but we've had to say some very hard things to her. Things about demons seeking to deceive her. Things about the devil masquerading as an angel of light. We've tried to say those things in humility. We've tried to say them lovingly. But you can imagine how hard it's been for her to hear some of those things. We've taken something that she's always thought of as a kind of intimate guardian, and we've called it a demon or a devil. It's been difficult for us to say these things to her, and we haven't said them lightly, but because we love her, we had to say these hard things to her. We couldn't say that we love her, and yet let her continue in deception by something that would ultimately keep her from the source of eternal life. Now, this isn't just an issue for missionaries on the mission field. All of us need to face it in our relationships with our non-Christian family members and friends, co-workers, and acquaintances. There's a strong temptation in our relationships to let things about God go unsaid. We don't want to stir up the dust by bringing up spiritual things. And I have to tell you that for us, it's very much the same as it is for you when we're back in America. When we're in Japan, we have a label. We're the missionaries, and people expect us to talk to them about God. But when we're in America, we blend in just like you do. And I know that that makes it a harder obstacle to overcome. Of course, we don't want to be prideful or forceful when we talk about spiritual things. But just like people in Japan who worship idols. Our friends and our family members face a terrible eternity if they remain apart from the God who will not give his glory to another. The stakes are very great for them, and if we really love them. Then we can't sit by quietly. We need to ask God to give us opportunities to talk to people to these people about spiritual things, and to give us the courage to take those opportunities when we have them. We also need to remember that God calls us to sow seeds and to harvest. He doesn't call us to cause those seeds to bear fruit. That's something that only God can do. And so the pressure is not on us to persuade our loved ones to believe. There's another reason why we had to say those hard things to Mrs. Inoue. And that's because God wants Mrs. Inoue's worship. And he wants it exclusively. Jesus told us that the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for they are the kind of worshipers the Father seeks. God seeks true worship from Mrs. Inoue. He doesn't want to share the glory that he is due with the idol of Mrs. Inoue's grandfather. And if God cares so much that his glory not be given to another, how can you and I not care? The passage that we read this morning is a messianic prophecy. It's the first of four passages called the Servant Songs, in which Isaiah prophesies about the Messiah that God will send In the same passage in which God says he will not give his glory to another, he tells us what he will do for the people who have turned away from him to idolatry. He will send his servant, who will bring justice to the nations. This servant will be a covenant for the people and a light for the Gentiles He will open blind eyes, set captives free, and release those in darkness. Now, since you and I can look back on this prophecy's fulfillment, we know that the God who speaks it is our Redeemer. It's he who loves us so much that he did not spare his own son in order to rescue us from the consequences of our sins. We once were his enemies in idolatry and in rebellion against him. And yet, as the Bible says, at just that time, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. This is one of the motivations that the Bible talks about for serving God. In 2 Corinthians chapter 5, it says that for Christ's love compels us. Because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died. And he died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him. Christ's love compels us. When we understand how much God loves us in Christ, we're overwhelmed, and we can't help but want to serve Him. If we truly love God, and if we truly want to serve Him, then what's important to God must be important to us. Sometimes I think that we're we're afraid that if we live by God's priorities, if we put the things that God puts pr priority on first in our lives, it'll mean that we won't have any happiness or enjoyment in life. But that kind of thinking is not correct. Jesus said that he came that we may have life and have it to the full. And we dishonor God if we make him out to be a hard and demanding taskmaster. We're not only his servants, but we're his adopted children. And he pours out abundant blessings on us. But if we're truly his servants, then it's inconceivable that we could not place great importance on something so important to him He's told us, I will not give my glory to another. And yet we see all around us a world that's ignoring him, not giving him the glory and worship that he's due. If we're truly his disciples, then we can't ignore the fact that millions are giving God's glory to another. It's happening right here in America, which is becoming increasingly secular. In fact, there's a growing tendency here not only to leave God out of people's private lives, but to exclude any reference to him in from public life as well. Since coming back to the U. S. last summer, we read in our newspaper about moves to remove the words One nation under God from the Pledge of Allegiance and about the removal of the Statue of the Ten Commandments from the courthouse in Alabama. And so the darkness is certainly growing darker right here in our own land. Ree and I were sitting in a doctor's office in the waiting room shortly after coming back to America. And sitting there with us was a father and his two young daughters. One of the daughters looked at him and said, Daddy? Why do you always have dark circles under your eyes? The father looked at her and said, well, that's the way God made me. Now to you, that may not seem like a very significant conversation. But I've been in Japan for eight years now. And I have never heard that kind of conversation in Japan. Never have I heard a Japanese parent explaining to their child about the God who made the world. Never in eight years have I seen a Japanese stranger bow his head and give thanks for a meal at a restaurant. Never in eight years have I met a Japanese Christian by chance on the street. The spiritual atmosphere here in America certainly is darkening. And yet there are many places around the world where it is so much darker. Outside America's shores, there are billions who are giving God's worship to spirits, to ancestors, to idols, to nature, or to nothing at all We can't ignore that. We've got to care and we've got to act. Practically speaking, what can we do? Well, all around us there are people who are not giving God the worship he seeks from them. In his final instructions to his disciples before returning to heaven, Jesus told them, You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem. and in all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth. He wanted them to begin right where they were. And the same is true for each of us. God has put us in a certain geographical location. He's put us in a certain family, a certain neighborhood, a certain school, a certain workplace. And in doing so, he's given us relationships with many people who are not giving his glory, who are giving his glory to another. As the Bible says, God gave us the ministry of reconciliation. That God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting men's sins against them. We are therefore Christ's ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. God is calling the people around us to be reconciled to Him, and He's calling them through us He wants us to be the ambassadors who are bringing his offer of reconciliation to the people that we have relationships with. And so we need to make sure in our daily lives that we are not insulated from non-Christians. There were many people in Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria who were not giving God the worship he was due. But there were a far, far greater number in other places. And there were far, far fewer people in those other places who could serve as God's ambassadors. The same is true today. The vast majority of people who are giving God's worship to another are geographically distant from us this morning. We need to be concerned about being ambassadors to those that God has put around us. But that doesn't mean that we can be unconcerned about those who are at the ends of the earth God wants their worship as well, and He's called us to be witnesses to them too. We can go, we can send, or we can disobey. We can go. But a point came where we realized that we couldn't say that we were followers of Jesus if we weren't willing to consider the possibility that he might want us to serve him overseas. Now I don't know each of you, and I don't know what God is calling you to do, but I'd like to encourage each of you to seek God and to ask him, how do you want me to be involved in bringing the gospel to the ends of the earth? You know, the world is a very different place than it was even 20 years ago. And being a missionary is also very different than it was. Perhaps you've heard of the 18th century century missionaries to Africa who packed all of their belongings in coffins before they went to the mission field because they knew that most of them were not coming back. Well, that's not the world that we live in. The world has changed, and world travel has changed with it, and there are so many possibilities today that were not available even a short time ago. To help you to envision what it might mean to go, let me share with you a couple of ways in which our missionary team in Japan uses short-term missionaries. But the thing I want you not to miss, Is that in many cases the first contact that those people have with Christians and with the Bible comes to a relationship with a short-term missionary who probably doesn't speak very much Japanese. Having another short-term missionary ready to join us at that time is very important to keeping the uh um Possibility of making new contacts going on. Another type of short-term missionary in Japan is a teacher at our school for the children of our missionaries. Our team has started its own small school because we realize that one of the biggest threats to our continuing presence in Japan is our children's education. At this school, in a given year, there are 15 to 20 students and two to three teachers. Of course, we're thrilled if we can have a certified teacher as one of our teachers. But that's not always the case. And yet some many years we've had just a general college graduate come and serve as a teacher. And occasionally we've had just a high school graduate come and serve as a teacher's assistant. Each year it's a challenge to find the teachers. And until this year, we've always found them. But this year, we were not able to find teachers for the school for our missionaries, for our children. And so three other members of the missionary team are teaching the children this year. One of them is our team leader's wife, Carol Iverson, who's been in Japan for 13 years and has a very fruitful ministry with Japanese women. Another is Linda Carner, who's also from Maryland, who's been in Japan for 12 years, and is our team's best Japanese speaker. Our children are a high priority to us, and so we're glad to have these people teaching our children. But the fact that they're teaching our children this year means that they've had to cut back very, very significantly on their ministry to Japanese people. So short-term missionaries who come to teach our children not only teach our children, but they also enable much ministry to Japanese people to take place. So sending a teacher to Japan is also like sending a Carol Iverson or a Linda Carner in addition to do ministry to Japanese. The highlight Anytime that we visit a church, the highlight is always meeting somebody who has been praying for us for years. And so my encouragement to you this morning is to seek God. Ask him to give you his heart for his glory. Our God in heaven, you are a great and glorious God. You're our maker, and you've given us our lives. And what I can imagine is that older, wiser Christians Looking on that 18-year-old with a knowing, older, wiser Christian look Maybe even a a smile on his face. Because what he's thinking to himself is brand new believer, you've no idea. Or you have very little idea. You have barely begun to grasp what you've just memorized. Because at this point, brand new believer, you have barely begun to grasp what this life is that you've just signed up for. Do you realize that what you've signed up for is a lifelong Christian life in which you walk with Christ in which the word of Christ is at work in you. And for the rest of your life, that word is going to be burning. In your life, burning away the dross of your own sins. For the rest of your life, that word is going to be hammering away. at the idols that you have taken 18 years to set up in your own heart. Do you have any idea what it is that you've memorized? And twenty-five years later, I think I have a slightly bigger idea. And Lord willing, twenty-five years from now, it'll be even bigger than it is today. And in fact, I suppose there's even a certain irony about this that we chose this verse to memorize, and it must have It must have been the case that we picked this verse in part because it inspired us to do the scripture memory that we were doing. Think about it. What were we doing? We were taking this word. That's fiery and mighty, burning and destroying. And we were deliberately taking that word and getting it as deeply rooted into our souls as we could get it. it. We were going out of our way to memorize a word that's like fire and a hammer. Who does that? Because look, there are all sorts of things you can memorize. And some people are better at memorizing things than others. For whatever reason, I've always been pretty good at memorizing things If you want, go for it. Memorize the periodical table of elements. But that's not going to burn. It may bore you to tears. But that's not going to burn like this. If you want, go ahead and memorize the capital cities of all the nations in the UN. Knock yourself out. But that's not really gonna hurt. But when you start memorizing scripture, you know what you're doing. You're taking a word that's like fire. taking a word that's like a hammer and you're saying that's the word I want. And I don't want it at a distance. I I don't want it just down the street at the library. I don't want it just sitting up on the shelf gathering dust. I want it in me. I want it to have free reign in me so that it burns. Burns away the dross of my own sin, hammers away at the idols of my own heart. And that doesn't just apply to scripture memory. You think about all of the ways in your life in which you're taking the Word of God and seeking to have it dwell in you richly. Every sermon that you hear. Every time you you read your Bible and think about what it ought to mean in your life, every time you read some book about the Bible so that you can grow in your grasp of it. Every time you sit down over a cup of coffee with a Christian friend and talk about Scripture, in every one of those situations, do you know what you're doing? You are handling fire. You are wielding a hammer. And you're doing it with this goal in mind that you should be forged. Fashion. That you should be made more and more like your Savior. So I want to challenge you this morning. Have you lost sight of this? Have you lost sight of how wonderfully dangerous is the Word of God in your life? If you have, I urge you to look to Christ. Look to Christ to learn again from Christ, to tremble at his word. And then for the very same reason, don't just tremble, but rejoice. This is great news. God has spoken And what he has spoken is a word that's not going to leave you as you are. I hope you don't want to be left as you are. And so it's very good news A fiery and mighty word. There's an interesting epilogue to this whole story. I I mentioned before that it was on the steps of Mopendorm on the grounds of UVA that I I sat down with those two friends that night, that morning, and prayed my very first. Real Christian prayer. Here's the epilogue. Mopendorm has since been torn down. A lot can happen in twenty-five years. Smashed into pieces. The way a hammer breaks a rock in pieces. I wasn't consulted. They just went ahead and did it. I never did join the Alumni Association. Maybe if I had, I'd have had more of a say. But they just knocked it down. And they knocked it down for a reason. And the reason was they were determined to put something new and improved in its place. And And I say I've no doubt that what's going up right now is going to be new and improved compared to the muffin I knew. Let me tell you, boys and girls, when I went to college. There were no amenities. Putting up a beautiful new moffendorm. But you see that's the point. Torn down. So that they could replace it with something far more glorious. Because there is a wielding of the hammer that is unto glory and not grief. There is a fire that burns not to consume but to refine and to make something beautiful. And brothers and sisters, that's what the Word of God, by the Spirit of God, by the grace of God, is doing in our lives. The word of God is fiery and it is mighty. And so for that very reason, don't run from it. Run to it. And take that fiery, mighty word and get it in. Get it in you. And watch it go to work. Amen. Let's pray together. Our Father in heaven, we tremble Because your word is fiery, it is mighty. And yet we tremble not as those who would run from it. But as those who would firmly grasp it, grant our grasp to be firmer, grant your word to be even more deeply rooted in us. May your word have free course in us, forging and fashioning us. To the praise of your glory, and we ask it in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Glen Knecht
sermons.text: I think one thing should be made clear at the outset. I was not present at the dedication of Solomon's temple. I had a conflict that day. I'm grateful to my friend Daniel Howard for uh giving me a little assistance on the steps. Uh what a blessing. I prayed that the Lord would send just the right message. man. I met him last Sunday. He said, Daniel, I have a job for you. Where are you, Daniel? There he is. Thank you. Let us pray for God's illumination upon our meditation today. Oh, spirit of truth Come and hover over us, over the word and the ministry of it, over our hearts, as we look to you for guidance, for teaching. For reproof, correction, and righteousness. Teach us, O Lord, and lift up our hearts. And And we do thank you for this pulpit and the messenger who stands in it. And we pray for him and his family as they undertake this new phase of their church's life. Anoint them With the Holy Spirit. In great measure, we pray. And anoint this time together, we ask in Jesus' name. Amen. It may be strange to put together in such juxtaposition the ministry of John the Baptist and the dedication. of this church. But I see a theme that ties them together, and I'd like to discuss that with you somewhat today The theme is this: that both of these, the Church of Christ and the Ministry of the Baptist Are to reflect the image of Christ to the world. They both have the same task So I looked under the guidance, I trust, of the Holy Spirit. What are some of the features? Of the similarity and the differences between the Baptist and Christ's Church, wherever it is found. I think if we can discover some of these features, it will help you as a church and me as a would-be pastor to Know and carry out the work of Christ as we are called to do. Let's think a little bit about the manner of John the Baptist's ministry. It was very different, wasn't it? Alone, fasting and praying in the desert. for 30 years with nothing to do otherwise but wait for the promised Messiah. and to prepare the heart for that, feeding on the locusts that had died in the crags of rocks, and the wild honey which a kind providence had put there for him It was a strange existence he had, far from humanity. But what that led to, I think, in John the Baptist was a profound humility. a kind of depth of humility that isn't seen in Scripture, apart perhaps from the prophet Elijah, in whose figure John the Baptist Seems to resonate. But this deep humility of his was a vital preparation for his ministry. It was essential. He was what was called a Nazarite, a person who had chosen vows for his life, usually temporarily. But in John's case, it seems to be his total life was given to the Nazarite Baal, which produced in him a concentration, a focus. On what he was called to do. It's an uncanny thing about humility that when it reaches its true point of depth in the soul It creates a focus on one's calling that can't be created any other way. Pride will spoil the focus and distract But not genuine humility. But John had that And it meant for him the depth of conscience because he In that humble state, received a sharp sensitivity in his conscience. He was better prepared to seek out and challenge the sins of the day. That aggravation of soul we call conscience. He felt keenly. He was, in a way, a man of sorrows before the true man of sorrows would appear. His manner, his humility is important to us as we think about the church. Think also about the message he brought, his purpose in the world. Was really to announce the coming of the king, to let as many know as possible that he was on his way. And to help them get ready for his coming. At the same time, what he wanted to do, it seems to me, was to create a people Who would be ready to recognize and receive the coming king? He had to create their hearts Make them ready to know Christ when he should appear and to respond to his message. Now, see comes. His message was really simple, twofold. Repent Be converted is what it means there. Change your ways. Change your life. In your present condition, you're in no shape to meet the king who comes. You need a drastic What we would call today a sea change in your life, a paradigm shift that you would be able to recognize him And respond to him. And the other part of his ministry, his message was The kingdom is at hand. The king is coming. He was to be a harbinger, a forerunner of the Savior's appearance, his advent. And that was important because there were huge obstacles in the way of the king and his reign. Obstacles like human pride, like dishonesty, like religious hypocrisy, all kinds of violence. The culture was not ready to hear a reformer, a changer, like the Savior, unless someone came. To lift up the low places and bring down the haughty and the proud, create a great leveling that would make a highway for our God to come. into the land. What a mission it was he had with that message. He wanted to minister In his coming to all kinds of people. The Pharisees and scribes had limited themselves to the learned, perhaps To the opulent, the wealthy. But John the Baptist cave is a humble and lowly man. He saw everyone as important in the eyes of God. So he had to lift up the poor and the fallen, the discouraged and those who had lost heart. He had to lift them up. And those who were high and mighty and lorded it over others, he brought them down. Those who were soldiers and thought themselves more powerful than others He also humbled them. All must be the same. And for that reason he chose three different titles For the king to come, so that everyone, wherever he was in the stations of life, would be able to relate to this Savior He called him the Son of God. What a universal title that was. And he called him the Lamb of God. So as to say that every man's a sinner and needs the sacrifice of the slain lamb, and here he comes And he called him the bridegroom. We're all interested in weddings. And The bridegroom was a unique ministry, a title that he gave to Jesus To attract people so that he could bring the people to Christ, that they would be drawn to him by that figure, so that everyone. Was interested in the message of John, and they came from every corner of the land to hear his words Now his method was different from others. His method was Interesting to us because he did not speak in generalities. Every preacher, including this one has to avoid that great hazard of being general when the folk want you to be specific And those of you who are seminarians and preachers of the Word will recognize what I mean when I say John the Baptist dude's particular application. That is, he singled out groups in his audience and spoke to them so directly that they squirmed in their places Nobody preaches such particular application. We're too busy and too hurried to take the time to do it. So we allow the particular application to be done by a counseling center somewhere instead of the pulpit where it needs to be done, it seems to me. But at least John the Baptist called certain groups vipers. They were sitting right there His fate in a certain sense was in their hands. The thing that was so different about his method, too, was that He didn't try to attract people to himself. Sometimes we pastors can do that maybe unconsciously at least at first, until we begin to get a certain joy about the hand club we have around us. Which leads more and more to our pride in being isolated from where people's real needs are. But not John the Baptist. He was as if to say, Don't come to me. I'm only the friend of the bridegroom. Go to the bridegroom. That's where the action is. He must increase. I must decrease. I'm only a voice. Now that's about as near to nothing as you can be, is to be just a voice. That's all I am is a voice. Don't come to me, don't flock around me Even his own beloved disciples, he shoved off to serve alongside the master when he came. And this sense of method was a very important way that he worked. You can see his hand, and we can emulate certain features of his life. And what we think of today as the church, What's wrong with us? Christ has come. The kingdom is not simply at hand. The kingdom is within you and within us. We live in the kingdom. We rejoice in the kingdom. We have much to preach. We have a message of repentance. And we can still say and believe with all our hearts the King is coming again. So while the Manner of John's asceticism is not honored in the New Testament. It's generally spoken of as being close to you. Useless. But John was an ascetic, to be sure. That's not the role. But we can take from his ministry a simple life. A detesting of luxury and fanfare and publicity so that we can live In a sense, a life detached unto God and yet attached to people in a deep and loving way. Now John's ministry, as the scripture readings we had point out clearly, was a transitory ministry It was a transition between the Old Testament and the New. And that's why Jesus says there, you rejoiced in his light for a season. It's not forever. John had that brief period of thirty years or so of ministry. And in that time the Lord Jesus said he was a burning and shining light. What a tribute. You who are pastors, would you not want Christ to speak of you that way? A burning? That is full of zeal and passion, not a ho-hum, haphazard servant of Christ. Anything goes But a burning light, and a shining light full of learning and teaching, full of illumination for your people, so that every Lord's day, when they sit before you, they are. Instructed, they go home with some new thought they never had before. Yet Jesus said he would pass away And of course, John's uncompromising stance against evil cost him his life. Because the day came when he Speaking to Herod, said of his desire to marry Herodias, his relative. He said You are not allowed to have her in public to a ruler So Don was like that amazing comet that goes across the sky, burning and beautiful, but it burns out, and he burnt out in prison. That's where he lost his head, as you remember. But now What our task as the church is, is to take from John the Baptist those features of his ministry, which are the essence of it. Old Testament. Teachings are so important because they have both a form and an essence. Ceremonial laws have that. Dunn's Ministry had the form, the outer form, which has passed away, but the heart of his message we can take and must take. For example, A lowliness of mind, a humility that John had. That will enable us to reach all kinds of people But too often we get stuck on our own programs and services and we get so routinized in the way we do things that we're inflexible to to meet the needs of those who are really hurting. It takes humility to be a church humble enough to reach every man. The city of Laurel may have more than its share of the homeless, the poor and the broken, the stranger. The handicapped. Somehow people have found their way here. And we want to be here. And we are here as churches to reach out and bless them. So we need the lowliness that John had. And I think we need also a fresh Glimpse of the cross. You remember the great hymn, lift high the cross? That's what we need to do. Because it was the death of Christ that was central in John's thinking about the Messiah. The first time he saw him, he was so struck with that face, utterly dedicated to its own suffering. That he said, behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Have we put up all kinds of subjects and themes and illustrations and stories, all these somehow bypassing The death of our Lord Jesus Christ. That's the remedy for human ills. That's the answer to society's hurt, is to preach Christ and Him crucified. And I think John the Baptist's message needs to be our message. Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. We can also take this leaf from John's notebook: the strength to be courageous against evil. We've gotten timid and maybe even defeatist in our struggle against social evils. And all kinds of wickedness in our society. But not John. He denounced it. He called it what it was. And we need to do the same. We need courage to do that. For example, take our national sins. John, I think my idea may be different from yours, but why did John baptize Jesus? That's a an enigma that people have wrestled with for a long time. I've kind of come out among at this place, among other reasons, not the only reason. was that both John and Jesus were citizens of the land. They were there, part of Israel, part of Palestine. And so, in a certain sense, as citizens, they participated in the national sins of the country. That doesn't mean Jesus was a sinner at all. Don't anybody misunderstand me? Of course not. But he was baptized, I think, to identify. And to say that he was going to take on the national sins of Israel. And are we too righteous and high and mighty to do that? We can condemn sins from the pulpit and in pronouncements. But can we repent with our neighbors, though we have never participated In these sins, can we repent for them and with our neighbors? That takes courage to do that We're now engaged in a war. And in a war, both sides are under the judgment of God. That's not to put ourselves in the same brutal category as ISIS With its barbaric hostility, merciless and relentless murder. No, never. Yet In a war, the victim, as it were, also suffers. As we know the suffering and pain. We're seeing it now. So that in a sense The victim nation has sins to repent of, as well as the aggressor. What are our national sins? That God may be calling our attention to in this time of terrible war I have a book in my library called Best Sermons. And I like to take it down. And when the war started to appear on the horizon, I read again. The great sermon of John Murray called God and the War, that would have been the Second World War. God and the War And he has an amazing sentence, then, which I've never quite wrapped my arms around. He said, one well-tept Sabbath would end this war. What? But you see, what Murray was saying was that there were national sins, one of which he was calling Sabbath desecration, one well-kept Sabbath. Would end the war. That's his sentence, not mine. Now you'll you'll have trouble now wrapping your minds around that one But you see, that's what I'm saying. Part of humility, part of playing out the ministry of John the Baptist in our contemporary world is to be able. To repent, identify with the sins of our nation, which are many. We don't participate. We refuse to do that But we do repent for them and with them. What else can we learn, briefly, from John the Baptist's ministry? Well, I think we need a whole new dependence and love of the Holy Spirit Because he said, the one who's coming after me, he will baptize you with the Spirit and with fire. He knew that the carnal sins of his land could not be washed away with the waters of Jordan. Oh, baptism had its place there. But it something deeper, something more powerful, something incendiary had to happen if the people were to change from their wicked ways. We need a new baptism of the Holy Spirit upon our churches, upon our ministries, upon our families. Please God, come, Spirit. Burn like the fire, cleanse like the water, refresh like the wind, but come, Holy Spirit, come. And I think John leads us to a fresh grasp of what it means to pray. Sometimes prayer in our churches can be perfunctory and rote and hardly expecting answers. Not long ago, Betty Jane and I met in a restaurant in Laurel, a young man from Nigeria, who had come to the U. S. as a refugee. Both parents, the only family he had, were killed by the Boko Haram there in the bombing of a bus. And here he was in America. And we met him and got to know him and loved him. But the feature of his life that so challenged me was his prayer life. What have you been doing, Opi? I spent the day in prayer. The whole day? Yes, the whole day And where have you been? We haven't seen you for seven days, Opi. Where have you been? I've been fasting and praying for seven days for my country. I'll tell you, my prayer life looked awfully shabby and paltry compared to that. But that wasn't the way John prayed. He prayed with an intensity and a depth. He prayed till his sinewy body was. Wet with sweat in the desert, seeking the coming of Christ, he prayed in the arrival of the Messiah. He brought him into the world by prayer. And we can hasten Christ's return, too, by our praying, if we will do so. So we need that, brothers. And somehow we need to go back and ask God for a a new conscience, a refreshed conscience One that is sensitive, not seared over by the worldliness and the sins of the age. I saw a video recently that brought this home to me. It was a video of a meeting, a reconciliation meeting between The Swiss Reformed churches and the Anabaptists of America, which would be the Amish, the Mennonites And evangelical Baptists, that group of plain people, of followers of Freelick and others in Switzerland Over 400 years ago, there had been awful persecution by the state church of these Anabaptist people and their leaders They had even drowned some of the leaders as a punishment for not baptizing their children. It's hard to conceive of that. But it was their own admission. We saw the video of this meeting in which These wonderful speeches of love and forgiveness and of confession of sin were made by these leaders of both churches. It was incredible. It was within the last ten years that this took place. There was the Lord's Supper together. There were tears of repentance. and forgiveness. There was the washing of one another's feet. I thought, ah The corporate conscience is being cleansed. There is such a thing as a body that has a conscience. And that body had its conscience so pinching it for its collective ancient sins that it had to be cleansed. And a church has a conscience. Your church has a conscience. Is it clear? Or are there those who have been burned May be treated poorly, not shown the love of Christ. Sometimes it seems that the megachurches are really made up of friends who've gotten rebuffed or didn't feel the love in some other churches. I don't know if that's true. But it seems that way sometimes. Have you examined your church's conscience? Before the Lord. The bloom that ought to exist on every congregation doesn't always come and thrive for this very reason Because we haven't cleansed our corporate conscience. Now let me leave you with a picture. In many devotional Christian books, not so much in recent publishing, but in earlier publishing, at the frontispiece there was a picture of Christ. And on one side was the disciple whom Jesus loved, John the Evangelist. And on the other side was John the Baptist. That was like an insignia on Christian books. You don't see it much. I have it. You may have it too. But I'm wondering with you today, friends, if we have studied and learned what John the Apostle has to give us, and it is so rich and so wonderful, no wonder we have majored on it. But have we neglected the ministry of John the Baptist and its austerity, in its keen sense of sin In its utter lowliness and humility. Perhaps it's time to rediscover what John the Baptist has to say to the church in this age. May we pray together? Our loving Heavenly Father, we thank you that in the sacred pages of the Scripture You have kept the words and ministry of John the Baptist for us, that we may study them and glean from them. How can the church reflect? The image of Christ to the world. Thank you for preserving his life, his ministry, his words for us. Lord, may we follow in his train through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

sermons.text: Morning, brothers and sisters at Christ Reformed Presbyterian Church. It's good to be with you again. We were last here in 2022, so it's been a few years. I think if I'm right, this is the tenth time we've been to this church. So we've seen you folks a few times. And it's always good to be with you. You've walked with us for many years now, and we've been greatly helped by your support, greatly upheld by your prayers. Greatly encouraged by hearing from you from time to time. It's been a joy for us to walk with you through many years, and we thank God for you. And it's a joy to be able to reconnect with you again today. Let's pray, and then I'll read today's passage, which is Philippians chapter 1, verse 6. Philippians chapter 1, verse 6. So let's pray. Father, we thank you that you are a God who draws near to us. Many people in the world, Japan included, think that you're very distant and have nothing to do with their daily lives, but that's not true. You're a God who draws near to us. You're a God who has spoken to us and left your word with us so that we can know you. So that we can know how it is that you're calling us to live, so that we can know about the way that you provided for us to be reconciled to you We're very grateful for your word. We pray as we interact with your word this morning that your Holy Spirit, who inspired that word, would enlighten our hearts. Give us faith to believe your word and power to live according to it. We pray. In Jesus' name. Amen. Okay, Philippians chapter one, verse six Whereby God's leading the Apostle Paul wrote this And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. Says God's word. As new missionaries, we got lots of advice from veteran missionaries. For example, we were told, don't you let yourself get sucked into ministry during your language study time. This was good advice, because the language aptitude that a missionary has at the end of their language study time is likely the language study that aptitude that they'll have for the rest of their career. It's a real temptation for us to get involved in ministry as soon as we can when we get to the field. Because we went to the mission field to do ministry. It's hard for us to be there and not to get involved. But by getting involved in the ministry too early, we don't make as much progress in the language, and this can limit our capacity for the rest of our careers. We were told, to learn a language, you have to make a million mistakes. So you better get started. That also was good advice. We've seen over the years that the factor that most determines how fluent a missionary will become is their willingness to make mistakes in front of other people. The missionaries who do their best with whatever vocabulary they have, knowing that they're probably making a lot of mistakes, those missionaries tend to reach a high level of fluency. Fluency. And those who are hesitant to speak until they're sure they've got it right tend not to become as fluent. And we were told, you'll be surprised at how little happens in a year, but you'll also be surprised at how much happens in ten years. I have to say that we didn't really grasp how profoundly true and important this advice was for some time. The point was that progress on the mission field is slow, but also that God is at work. We had to experience some of the frustration of the slow progress before this advice really resonated with us. But then, in time, we began to see that the second part was also true. We'd reached a point where we could look back and see that God actually had been at work and that he had brought about more than we had realized. Actually, this last piece of advice was initially hard for us to accept. Maybe such advice is hard for many people to accept. We want to see results quickly. We're often in a hurry. Maybe it's because we're Americans, and Americans are very goal-oriented and expect to see results. Or maybe it's because we live in an age of amazing technology in which I can contact you instantly on your cell phone, even though I'm on the other side of the world. We've become used to rapid results. But it seems that God is not in a hurry. He has his plans for what he intends to accomplish, but he isn't in a hurry to do so. Consider, for example, his words to the serpent in the garden. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel. Genesis 3. 15. But even by the most conservative estimates, It was 4,000 years before Jesus, the offspring of the woman, appeared on earth to bruise the head of the serpent. And when Jesus ascended to heaven 40 days after his resurrection, the angel told his disciples, this Jesus who is taken up from you into heaven, will come in come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven. Acts 1. 11. Some of Jesus' followers expected that Jesus would return to establish his kingdom in all its fullness on earth during their lifetimes. But nearly two thousand years have passed since these words were spoken. God had a plan to send a Savior, and He's done so. And God has a plan to establish His kingdom on earth, and He'll do so. But he clearly hasn't been in a hurry in either of these cases. Perhaps he's not in a hurry to bring some of his other plans to fruition as well. There's a verse which reminds me of some important foundational truths which help me to have a right perspective on God's work in me, in my own life, and on God's work in the world around me. In Philippians 1. 6, the Apostle Paul wrote, And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. One thing I should say at the outset. When Paul wrote to the believers in Philippi that God began a good work in you, the word you is plural in the original. That means that the truth that's taught in this verse doesn't apply only to us as individuals. I'm not saying that it doesn't apply to us as individuals. I believe it does I'm saying that the truth taught in this verse was relevant to both the whole community at the church at Philippi and also to each individual member of that community. God has begun a good work in that community. And God has begun a good work in each member of that community. And God will bring each of those works to completion. These are words which give us hope. God is at work. He's doing a good work. And when God is at work, there's reason for us to have hope. These are also words which give us confidence. God will bring the good work he's begun to completion. When God starts a work, he finishes the work that he's started. And these are words which call us to patience. Bringing his good work to completion is something that will take until the day of Jesus Christ. God's work isn't finished yet. It will be finished, but at present it's still a work in progress. So when we notice that there's still more progress needed in God's work in us or in God's work in the world around us, we shouldn't be surprised. We shouldn't become complacent. We should remain hopeful and confident. But we should also recognize that God's work being remaining unfinished will be the normal state of things until Jesus comes back. Let's first think about God's work in individuals. God has begun a good work in each person who trusts in Jesus. What is that good work? We can find the answer to in another passage which Paul wrote. And we know that for those who love God, All things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his son in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called. And those whom he called, he also justified And those whom he justified, he also glorified. Romans 8, 28-30. The work that God is doing in each of us is the work of conforming us to the image of his Son. God is transforming each of our hearts to make us more and more like Jesus. This is the work of sanctification. And notice where the work ends. We're glorified. We're made completely like Jesus. That's the completion of the work that God does in each of us. But God's work in us isn't finished yet. I often see the stark reality of the need for further transformation in my own life Far too often, it's my old self which comes out rather than the new self into which God is making me. Far too often, it's apparent that I'm serving myself rather than serving God. Do you experience some of these same things in your life? When we see such things in our own lives, it's important that we take them seriously. We need to acknowledge the sinful tendencies which remain in our hearts, to lament them, and to repent of them. But at the same time, we should have hope. God has begun a good work in us. That work isn't finished yet, and at times we see evidence that more transformation is needed. But God will finish the work he's begun in us. He won't leave us as we are. God is not only at work in us, he's at work in individuals, other individuals around us as well. Perhaps there are some people that you know in whom you notice the need for further transformation. Maybe some family members. Maybe some people with whom you work closely. Maybe some people in your church. The same things are true of those people that are true of us. If they trusted in Jesus, then God has begun a good work in them. God's work in them isn't yet complete, so it's natural that there would be times when we see evidence of the need for further transformation. But God will finish the work that He's begun in them. Let me tell you the story of a young man we know in Japan. I'll call him Junji, but that isn't his real name. Junji grew up in a church-going family. However, in his teen years, he became disillusioned with the church. There were several reasons, including some things related to his own heart, but one reason for his disillusionment was hypocrisy that he saw in the people who attended the church. Their lives didn't match their words. Junji eventually stopped attending church. He disassociated himself from all fellowship and began pursuing his own interests. He made some lifestyle choices that weren't the best. After graduating from high school, he started working a job. But God didn't leave Junji in that place. After working for a while, Junji realized that he didn't want to be doing this kind of job for the rest of his life. He thought he'd have more options if he went to college. So he began investigating his options. Just at this time, Junji heard about an open campus event that was being held at a Christian college. It's probably a little surprising that he would even consider a Christian college because of his earlier disillusionment with the church. But he went to that open campus event. He found that the tuition at this Christian college was lower than many other colleges. And because of some financial limitations his family was facing, The lower tuition was a significant factor. So Junji applied to and was accepted by this Christian college. Some of the things that Junji was hearing in his college classes really began to strike him. In particular, the words of Jesus recorded in Mark 2. 17 had a profound impact. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. Junji began to understand that the people at his church were a work in progress. Of course they sometimes fell short. And he knew that he too was far from perfect, that he needed the forgiveness that Jesus offered, and God's transforming power in his own life. So Junji came back to faith in Jesus. The students at this Christian college are required to do Sunday internships at area churches. And so this requirement brought Junji to the church that I was pastoring, Shin Urayasu Grace Church, and he served there as an intern. In time, he became a member of the church. Then he became a deacon in the church and contributed greatly by serving in a wide variety of ways He married a woman who was also a member of the church. And several months ago, we sent Junji and his wife off to become church staff at a new church plant. The transformation in Junji's life covered a period of about 10 years, and there were some low points along the way. But God carried on the work that he had begun in Junji, and the transformation is evident. Philippians 1. 6 invites us to have hope for others we know as well. God is at work in them, just as he's at work in us. He won't leave them where they are. He will finish his work in them. But Philippians 1. 6 also calls us to patience, recognizing that God's work of transformation in people we know is still in process, just like it's still in process in us. So let's believe the promise of Philippians 1. 6. Let's believe it for ourselves. Don't lose hope. Keep persevering to put off your old self and to put on the new self. Keep trusting that God is carrying out the work that He's begun in you. And let's believe the promise for others as well. Don't lose hope that God is at work in them. Keep praying for them as you wait expectantly for God to further his work of transformation in them. Now let's think about God's work in the community of his church. What's the work that God is doing in his church Jesus said to Peter, I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Matthew 16, 18 That's the work that God is doing. Building the church of Jesus Christ, establishing the kingdom of God. When Jesus spoke of building his church, he was speaking of his worldwide church. To borrow the words of the Westminster Confession, in fact the chapter that you just finished, This worldwide church consists of the whole number of God's chosen people who have been, are, or will be gathered into one under Christ, the head of the church. That's the church which Jesus is building. That's the church against which the gates of hell cannot prevail. Several years ago I had the opportunity to visit the ruins of Ephesus in modern-day Turkey. I was able to see The theater at which a crowd gathered in opposition to the message which the Apostle Paul was preaching. There are the remains of a house in which it's said that the Apostle John lived with Mary, the mother of Jesus. carrying out the commission to care for her given to him by Jesus from the cross. But there's no active church in Ephesus now. The thriving church of the New Testament times is no longer there. But while individual churches may come and go, the worldwide church of Jesus Christ will always be. As that same chapter in the Westminster Confession says, there will be always a church on earth to worship God according to his will. In each individual church, there will be times of progress and there'll be setbacks. But God is doing a work among us of building his church, building the church of Jesus Christ God is establishing his kingdom, and he will finish that work. There will be a church of God's people for eternity. God will rule over his kingdom forever. And each of us is a part of that work in our various locations. The Church of Jesus Christ is being built around the world. God's kingdom is expanding right here in Laurel. It's expanding in Japan and in other places. And each of us is a part of that work. But we don't produce the results As the Apostle Paul said, I planted, Apollo slaughtered, but God gave the growth. God has begun this work, and God will finish this work. We may plant and we may water, but it's God who produces the growth. It's been said by some that ministry in Japan is like plowing in concrete. That's because of the small percentage of the population in Japan, which are evangelical Christians. The Joshua Project is an organization which measures the growth of the church and the growth of God's kingdom around the world. And they estimate that 0. 4% of Japanese are evangelical Christians. And so more than 165 years after the first Protestant missionaries arrived in Japan, there's still only one out of every 250 Japanese who are evangelical Christians. By comparison, that same Joshua Project estimates that 26. 6% of Americans are evangelic Christians, or one out of every four. Actually, our experience is that it's much easier to get a hearing for the gospel with non-Christians in Japan than it is here in the United States. That's because Japanese people don't assume that they already know what Christianity is. So they're curious and they're willing to learn. But the pressure to conform in Japanese society is very strong, and Japanese people are very slow to change as a result. They're very hesitant to become different than other Japanese. Probably the question we've been asked the most as we visited churches is, why are there so few Christians in Japan when there's been such a good response to the gospel in Korea? There are several answers to this question. The isolation of Japan as an island nation means that it's a very homogeneous place. And so it's much harder to be different when everyone around you is the same. The prosperity of Japan means that the sense of need in Japanese people has been somewhat. And the position of strength which Japan has occupied in Asia is very different than the posture of humility which is needed to receive the gospel. But ultimately, revival is a work of the Holy Spirit, and the wind blows where it wishes. John 3. 8 There has been revival in Japan a few times in the past. In the 1870s, revival broke out in response to the concerted prayer of missionaries and Japanese Christians. And especially in the cities of Yokohama, Sapporo, and Kumamoto, significant numbers of Japanese people came to faith. In the first five years of the 20th century, there was another revival that broke out, and again it was in response to concerted prayer. And in that revival, the membership of the Japanese churches almost doubled. And in the aftermath of World War II, a humbled and broken Japan saw a large number of people turn to Christ. And out of this revival, a large number of pastors were raised up as well. Perhaps you notice the connection between concerted prayer and revival. We're praying for another revival to come to Japan. A broader revival to come to Japan. Please join us in this prayer. And we're praying with hope and expectancy, because when God begins a work, he carries it on to completion. God is working in Japan, just as he's working in Laurel. And all of us have an ongoing part in his work. So let's believe the promises of Philippians 1. 6 for God's work in the world around us. Let's not become discouraged and lose heart. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain. First Corinthians 15, 58. Jesus is alive. God has given us victory through Jesus. And God will finish his work. So let's keep planting and keep watering. Keep planting and watering here in Laurel and keep planting and watering around the world through your prayers and your giving, and hopefully by sending some from your own congregation. And let's trust God to give the growth. And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. Philippians 1. 6 calls us to have hope. God is at work in us and in the world around us. It calls us to be confident. God will finish his work. And it calls us to be patient, knowing that God's work isn't yet finished, and to wait expectantly as he continues his work. Let's pray. Father, we thank you that you are a proactive God, a God who took initiative and has made a way for us to be reconciled to you. We thank you that by your Holy Spirit you took the initiative to begin a good work in those of us who trust in you. And we thank you that you are committed to carrying on that work and to bringing it to completion. And so we pray that you would carry on the work that you're doing in each of us. Helping us more and more to be conformed to the image of your Son. And we pray that you would carry on the work that you've begun in the world, building the Church of Jesus, establishing your kingdom. These are your promises, and we hold to them with confidence, and we pray that you would finish your work to your glory in Jesus' name.
